Firstly, I'm going to try and keep the matter in public session, so that those people who are interested in this case can watch and listen to it, which means that I'm going to do everything possible to avoid revealing your identity to the public. Will you do the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To try to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Avoid revealing your identity to the public, so that means don't refer to your name or anybody you know or anywhere you might have lived. That sort of thing. Okay? And the second thing I'd like you to do for me is to listen to my questions and see if you can answer them shortly. Because we haven't got much time left, and it will get it over with quicker. Okay? Now, the first area of questions I have to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the first area of questions I've got for you are about your work within the Zvornik Brigade. So again, here, be careful and think about what you're saying and don't reveal too much about your identity. But I'm going to suggest to you that your work at the Zvornik Brigade meant that you came into regular contact with many soldiers, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, you drove them by the busload, didn't you, for a long period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that doesn't mean that I had contacts with them. It's a routine kind of work. Some soldiers were perhaps a bit irritable or drunk. I could recognise them. I knew them by sight. When you know someone then you know their name, you know who they are, where they're from. They all knew me, excuse me, but I just knew them very...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am perfectly happy with the answer that you have given me. You have probably saved me three or four questions. But also you were at the Standard building the headquarters at Karakaj on virtually a daily basis, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the place -- or rather, that's the place where I had to come. I would hand over the car there, and then leave. Mainly that's it. I didn't have any other command post or any place where I was bound to report for duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, thank you. And, generally speaking, it wasn't always the case, but generally speaking you would arrive for work in the morning and you would finish by dropping the car off in the late afternoon or early evening, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if on occasion you arrived much later than that, you would be pretty lucky to run into your transport manager, wouldn't you, because he would have gone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They worked in shifts. I always had to hand over the car to someone, so that they would know that I left the car in a working condition, washed, with all the papers. If they were there, perhaps the person was sleeping on the bed, and I would have to wake them up. Sometimes people would come at 1.00 in the morning, 3.00 or 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on, and remind you of a particular day when according to the records we've seen, you did go to the Standard building. That was the 4th of July. Now, I don't suppose you will remember this day, but it was a day when a -- a military force left the Zvornik Brigade headquarters on a combat mission.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know that there was a departure, a movement, because there weren't too many soldiers at the barracks. They were all outside, so you didn't really see that much activity in terms of vehicles. If anything like that happened, you would of course sense it and know it was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And did you know or come to know through speaking to people at the barracks that that was a force that was going on a combat mission under the command of Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Can I just go into a little bit more detail? Not much. Can I, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as for Mr. Pandurevic, please excuse me, but I feel that I have the right to say that Mr. Pandurevic, until he is convicted, as far as I'm concerned for me, and I think also before God, I can take that right. That whole situation in Srebrenica and during the events in Zvornik and around Zvornik, believe me, everyone in the barracks asked themselves where is "Zuti." Please don't mind me saying this. It's a nickname used by friends, and Mr. Pandurevic wasn't around to hear it. They would refer to him as "Zuti." That's when you think something well of a person. Everybody thought -- because that man was very capable and intelligent, incredible, a very rare example of a man of such abilities of him evading such a situation, avoiding it. He was on sick leave, studying, taking exams. He either took his Ph.D. or his masters or something like that. Everybody was talking, Well, he knew how to get himself out. How to extricate himself. This is something that everybody in the barracks was talking about. Since nobody saw him at the barracks, heard of him, that's why people were saying what's happening with him. They said he left the hot coals to Dragan Obrenovic. He was so clever that he managed to get himself away. I don't know how that -- how much of that story is true. That's something that God knows, other people perhaps know, witnesses or perhaps Mr. Pandurevic. But it's a man who -- there was no person in the barracks that had any reason not to love and respect him. Well, you don't have to love him, but you would respect him. He solved a million situations that no officer would be able to solve. Difficult situations, difficult problems, he would resolve them. They would call Pandurevic. He would sit there for an hour, five hours with a large number of people to resolve a situation without shouting, without any kind of imposition or screaming like officers have a habit of doing. I'm sorry, but I just felt that I needed to say something about a man that I knew. It is my sacred duty to do that. I was never in a situation to say "Good day" to this person and I regret that. I wish I could have experienced some contact with him, just like maybe with an artist or some major figure or something. I'm sorry, and I regret and my heart will ache if it should turn out - I don't know - but if he is in a situation to be called to responsibility. Well, I'm sorry. This is what I wanted to say, and I'm sorry if I was a little bit too expansive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much. I was simply going to ask you to confirm for me that from the 4th of July, and including the period when you went to Orahovac or say you went to Orahovac, Vinko Pandurevic was not in and around the command headquarters. I think you've confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I am speaking the truth, before God and before people and before this Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the other factor that you have confirmed for me is that during the period we are talking that is relevant to your evidence, the command of the brigade was the responsibility of Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That was the situation. I was in the circumstances where I was sent off with bales of nylon to take to Obrenovic on the Serb side where Obrenovic was located with Pragas and self-propelled canons, guns. And I was in a situation where I had to go through the corridor via Crni Vrh made by the people from Srebrenica. Only God and they allowed me to cross the corridor. I went through that corridor of theirs, which was very, very intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to move on to another subject, but before I do I am going to have to just drop into private session for just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back to open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to remind you of the details of what you said. You said you saw about 30 prisoners in total. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And they were in a hall that was fit for holding 130 people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment. In a room, yes, but the prisoner -- the prison was also used for Serb soldiers before and after that. Those people who were there, the 20 or 30 people were not people who had been taken to executions. They were there, one, two, three days. The buses were arriving, soldiers came out of the buses with their hands tied, then their blindfolds were taken off. They went to the bathroom; that was why they stopped there. They were escorted there. Normally, none of them stayed there or remained there for any period of time during the day. Perhaps I saw three buses. At the times when I was at the barracks, these were buses with Vukovar, Novi Sad licence plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please try and keep the answers short. I'm trying to keep the questions simple. You said there were five or six in another room, which you described as a toilet. Can I put something to you: The room you're talking about is, in fact, a holding cell with a small wash basin and some mattresses in it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a cell, sir. It's a toilet; classical bathroom, toilet, sink. I don't know if there were mattresses there or not, but they were locked. The door was not open like it was with the -- these 20 or 30 people. I guess some of those 20 or 30 people were allegedly described as extremists and that's where they were placed. They took their food there. These were separate from the other ones. I don't know what the reasons for that were, but they were not mistreated either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have said somewhere in your answer - I'm afraid I've lost my LiveNote - but you said somewhere in your answer that you thought these people were held there for two or three days. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I saw them there one day, and I was in the situation that when I carried out an assignment or something I would go back there. You know, these are difficult situations, difficult experiences, and then you come to see something that you've never seen in your life and then you talk to them as if they were your own people. And these police officers were sitting inside and speaking with them, these two or three local policemen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the occasion on which you saw these prisoners in the room and in the toilet at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters was a different day to the day on which you went to Orahovac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The buses and all of this was earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to suggest to you, you are wrong about that. It was on a different day. It was, in fact, later than the day you went to Orahovac, wasn't it? Do you think that might be possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the buses were before Orahovac, because I know I saw one man from Konjevic Polje who was there. His name was Omer. He was a tyre man and he was waiting in a line to go into the -- to the toilet, and the man said to me, "Can you help me?" And I told him there is no way, I was afraid for my own life. "If I help you, I just dare not. I simply dare not. And perhaps you are going to be exchanged, and I have no reason to help you."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you subsequently hear that the people who had been held there had been exchanged. They'd been taken to Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can only assume so. I did not ask around, believe me. The impression was these were important people who had something to tell, and they were being held there. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). I know he was held and killed -- or rather, he was held and interrogated and then he was released; and when he was released, he reflected positively on the time of his detention. I suppose these people were held there in the interests of further investigation, and were then transferred to Bijeljina to that prison, whatever it's called, from where they were either exchanged or...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to ask you one more question, and I want you to think very carefully about it. I've probably asked it before, but it's a long time ago now. And the reason I did ask you the question about where the funeral was in relation to Orahovac is to illustrate to you how difficult it is to place these events in time. Do you think it is possible that you saw the buses after you went to Orahovac rather than before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He's answered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered that question, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't believe he has addressed the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He asked if it was possible and he said, "I don't think so."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go through it again one more time, and this will be the last time. Witness, do you allow for the possibility that you may have seen the buses after and not before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, and I'm convinced, that I saw them before the execution at Orahovac. Where the buses went on from there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You will be glad to hear I'm coming to my last topic of cross-examination for you, and I want to return to something that Mr. Bourgon has asked you about. And it's about taking the boy to the hospital. I want to ask you when it was, and this better be in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You would agree, wouldn't you, that Mali Zvornik is a short distance away from Zvornik itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that Celopek is, in fact, a suburb of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And these are destinations that you regularly placed upon your vehicle log to explain where you had been driving on any particular day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that Orahovac, by contrast, is about ten kilometres from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not ten. It's not ten. It's, I think, maybe even closer than Celopek.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Haynes. Who is next? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have only several questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to remind you of one part of your testimony that I read, which says that at the point that you arrived at the execution site, you were addressed by a soldier who told you that in another meadow there were executions carried out, that other meadow was full of corpses, that they stopped firing upon people there, and that they moved to that other meadow where you were located at the time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood you to say that for the time you spent there, as you arrived at the site, it was still day-time. There was no sun, but there was daylight. You were able to see clearly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to tell you that we had occasion to hear the testimony of one witness here who fortunately survived an execution at this other meadow behind. The witness told us that the executions finished over there at nightfall, and that the people who were involved in that there only then went over to this other meadow where you said that they were firing at the time. I'm merely trying to point to you this contradiction; because based on the statement of this witness, and we have no reason to disbelieve him, the executions were transferred to the meadow where you were at night, and not during the day when, as you say, you arrived there, you arrived there at dusk, but it was still light, as you said it. I want to ask you whether you stick to what you said before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I believe that this man had darkness, saw darkness because of what was happening. Because as I arrived there, the sun went -- had gone down, because you know that the sun sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. At any rate, you are claiming that this was done in the daylight and that you were able to see everything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as these events progressed, it was getting darker and darker, and I told you that I switched the lights on for the child with a reason, to allow him to see and to be able to talk to him as a father would. This is where the -- this pile of corpses was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Already at the time when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this boy, because this part had been done away with before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to belabour the point, as you've already discussed it the extensively.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, your microphone is not turned on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Fortunately, there were a few others who survived the executions at that very site where you were, and their stories seemed to be consistent as to the time until which the executions at this other site were taking place because there was mention of flashlights that they used.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I told I that I -- I am convinced that after I left, they continued executions under flood lights.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we misunderstood each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, our time is over. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know how much more my friend has, or whether anybody else has anything, but it's just a few minute, I would implore everybody to see if we could stay just a few more that so that we're done. Fore the sake of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a re-examination to start with?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many -- how much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I would need some ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Beara team?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would have no questions for this witness. We gave our time to Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Borovcanin team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Miletic team?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it. The Gvero team, I under have already indicated that they don't wish to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go a few more minutes. Try to -- I don't think there is a sitting this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Go ahead and please try not to overstep the ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that we didn't understand each other. I said that after this execution, the executions continued on the other meadow to fill up the ranks of the guards, not at this meadow where you were. This is what I was thinking. So, however, you think that perhaps it was continued here and that's all right. Something else, let me tell you. Besides this witness that we had the opportunity to hear here, we had the opportunity to hear another witness who survived, and there are statements of two other survivors whose statements for the most part corroborate each other. And this is why I put that to you, because as you say, this one saw darkness before his eyes and was unable to see, that it was actually dark.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not funny. This is sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, no, I'm not laughing. It's just that I cannot believe that the four of them could have made such a mistake, whether it was during daylight or night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-101 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well then I'm lying, then I must be lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are moving at a terrific speed. Please allow -- allow a pause between question and answer, otherwise you will create a hell of a confusion here. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is more argument than asking questions, because the witness has answered the question and then he's making his argument, which is fair at the right time. But I don't think it's -- it needs to be done with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think Mr. Nicholls is right. The witness was there for a limited period of time. That's what he can testify about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I am not going to continue with my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It becomes a question of argument later on. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just for the record, I believe on line 14, page 89, the witness stopped his answer at, "I'm not laughing," and then I think the question started, "It's just that, I cannot believe that the four of them ..." It looks likes one whole answer -- one whole question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you for that. It needs to be attended to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. You are right, Mr. Meek, and thank you for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it ought to stay as it is, because it is Mr. Zivanovic after all who said, "No, I'm not laughing." So that brings us -- yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President, I look at the transcript on page 90, when you address my colleague, and you said the witness was there for a limited period of time. Mr. President, this has been our case since the beginning, this witness was not on that site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I meant to say, according to what he said, obviously. We have concluded our business with you. You are free to go. You will be attended to by our staff. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for coming over to give testimony here, evidence in this case. I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding. I'm sorry if I made any mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I understand you wanted to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, just on a logistics matter. I have spoken to Defence counsel and because of some issues that have arisen with Dr. Haglund, we are -- I believe we've agreed that he will come on in about two weeks, not in the next one or two witnesses as planned. And I wanted to confirm that with everyone and alert the Trial Chamber to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would that mean that Stefanie Frease would enter in that lot immediately after PW-105.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We just want to make sure that is known to everyone. All right. We have concluded for the day. We wish you a good weekend. And Monday, we will be -- shall we do the exhibits now or on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Do we do the documents Monday or now? I have no preference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can do it now. We can do it now, on the assumption that there are not going to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would prefer, Mr. President, if we wait until Monday because I will ask for some of the statements to be admitted for impeachment purposes but redacted -- in a redacted form. So I would prefer if we wait until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will do that on Monday. Monday, we will be sitting in the afternoon, exceptionally; and throughout the rest of the week we will always be sitting in the afternoon next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Except Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Except Friday, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of February, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.53 p.m.,
